title: The Wardian case: how a sealed glass box moved living plants, and the pests it carried

sources.title: The Wardian Case: How a Simple Box Moved the Plant Kingdom (Luke Keogh, Arnoldia 74(4), 2017)
A little world within a world: The Wardian Case of Tropical Ferns in the Victorian Home (Molly K. Eckel, 2017)

sources.publisher: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach (Yard and Garden)
sources.title: How to Create and Care for a Terrarium

facts.text: In 1819 John Livingstone, an East India Company surgeon stationed in Macao, estimated that only about one in a thousand live plants shipped from China to London survived the voyage.
Before the Wardian case, live plants were commonly just packed in boxes and loaded onto ships; the botanist John Lindley criticized this practice in 1824.
In 1829 Nathaniel Bagshaw Ward, a London physician, buried a sphinx moth chrysalis in moist soil inside a sealed glass bottle; the moth never emerged, but a fern and some meadow grass sprouted.
Ward lived in Wellclose Square in London's East End, where the polluted air had poisoned the plants he tried to grow; glass cases shielded plants from that outside air.
The grass and fern in Ward's sealed bottle survived for about three years without being watered.
In a closed glass container, water released through plant leaves collects as droplets on the glass and runs back down to the soil, where the plants can use it again.
In 1833 Ward sent two sealed glass cases holding ferns, mosses and grasses by ship from London to Sydney; all but three of the plants arrived alive.

In February 1834 the cases were refilled with Australian plants; the return voyage took about eight months, through temperatures from over 30 degrees C to about -7 degrees C near Cape Horn, and the plants reached London healthy.
Ward described his method in the 1842 book On the Growth of Plants in Closely Glazed Cases; his wood-and-glass boxes became known as Wardian cases.
The nurseryman George Loddiges put more than 500 Wardian cases into circulation around the world.
Botanical gardens and nurseries used Wardian cases to move crops such as tea, rubber, cinchona and bananas to new regions where they were grown.
Ferns in Wardian cases became fashionable in middle- and upper-class Victorian homes; the Wardian case is an early form of the modern terrarium.
Because Wardian cases contained soil, plants arrived with insects and plant diseases, and stowaway seeds in the soil sprouted.
In 1862 George Rogers Hall, an American physician, returned from Japan with Wardian cases that included Japanese honeysuckle; the vine later invaded woodlands across the eastern United States.

In 1924 Beverley Galloway, chief of the US Department of Agriculture's Bureau of Plant Industry, warned that Wardian cases had probably spread more harmful insects, nematodes and other pests than almost any other carrier.
Plant quarantine rules grew stricter; Wardian cases were largely out of use by the 1940s, and the last ones were used in the 1960s, when plastic bags and air freight replaced them.
Air transport allowed live plants to be shipped quickly without soil, wrapped in plastic.
Derived: Wardian cases were in wide use for roughly a hundred years, from Ward's 1842 book to their decline by the 1940s.

notes: Sources differ on how long the plants in Ward's first bottle lived without water (about three years in s1, four in other accounts), so the passage says only 'for years'.
